# Bid Rigging, Shapes of Bids and Machine Learning {#sec-bidshape}

The Public Works Department of a State lets several hundred road and building works every year. Many of these works are large. A State highway, a district hospital block or a bridge may attract five, eight or even ten bids. Such a tender looks healthy. Many firms took part, and the lowest bid won. But a group of firms can arrange even a tender with eight bids. One firm is chosen to win. The others put in cover bids, a little above the winner and close to each other. The file shows eight bidders, and the department pays the price the group agreed.

The previous chapter, @sec-bidrig, looked for such groups by following firms *across* many tenders. This chapter looks *inside* each tender, at the shape of its bids. When firms compete, their bids spread out, because their costs and their keenness differ. When covers are arranged, the losing bids tend to bunch together, well above the winner. Researchers in competition economics have turned this idea into a set of simple measures called **screens**. They have also trained machine learning models on the screens, using tenders of cartels that were later proved.

This chapter teaches the screens, shows what the research says they can and cannot do, and builds a random forest on them. It is honest about two limits. The screens need four or more bids, so they do not work on small tenders. And a model needs *labels*, tenders already known to be collusive or competitive, which real audits rarely have. This is the third of three chapters on tenders. The first, @sec-tenderflags, checks the tendering process itself.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Our data, five years of larger works tenders {#sec-bidshape-data}

We have the tenders of the Public Works Department of an imaginary State for 2020-21 to 2024-25. There are 880 road and building works in five made-up circles, Rajgarh, Sonepur, Tilakpur, Udaygiri and Vasantnagar. Sixty made-up firms, `K01` to `K60`, took part. These are larger works, so most tenders received four to ten bids.

There are two tables.

- `bids` has one row for each bid. It records the tender, circle, type of work, date, financial year, estimated cost and bid amount in ₹ lakh, the number of bids, the firm, the rank of the bid (1 is the lowest), whether it won, and a column `collusive`.
- `truth` says, for each tender, which cartel was behind it, if any, and whether genuine outsiders also bid.

The column `collusive` needs a word. Because the data is simulated, we *know* which tenders were arranged. This is a **label**, and a model needs labels to learn from. Real audits rarely have such labels. A label exists only after an investigation has proved a cartel. We come back to this in @sec-bidshape-responsible. The table `truth` is kept aside, and we use it only to check how well each method did. An auditor would never have it.

The code is folded. Genuine bids spread more widely in some tenders than in others, so some genuine tenders look tight by chance. Three cartels have been planted.

1. **Cartel A** of six firms works in Rajgarh from April 2020 to September 2022. When it bids alone, the chosen winner bids above the estimate. The covers sit 1.5 to 4.5 per cent above the winner and are bunched within about 1 per cent of each other.
2. **Cartel B** of seven firms works in Tilakpur from April 2022 to March 2025. It is a little sloppier. Its covers are spread over a wider band.
3. **Cartel C** of five firms works in Udaygiri from July 2021 to June 2024. It is an **incomplete cartel**. In every one of its tenders, one or two genuine outsiders also bid. The members then bid lower, to have a chance against the outsiders, but their covers are still bunched.

Cartels A and B also meet an outsider now and then.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the tender data"
set.seed(2026)

circles <- c("Rajgarh", "Sonepur", "Tilakpur", "Udaygiri", "Vasantnagar")
firms <- sprintf("K%02d", 1:60)
firm_habit <- setNames(round(rnorm(60, 0, 1.2), 2), firms)

# The firms that usually bid in each circle
pools <- list(
  Rajgarh     = sprintf("K%02d", c(1:14, 55:57)),
  Sonepur     = sprintf("K%02d", c(15:26, 1, 2, 58)),
  Tilakpur    = sprintf("K%02d", c(27:38, 15, 16)),
  Udaygiri    = sprintf("K%02d", c(39:48, 27, 28, 59, 60)),
  Vasantnagar = sprintf("K%02d", c(49:60, 39, 40, 3))
)

# Planted. Three cartels, each active in one circle for a period.
# cover_gap is how far (per cent) the first cover sits above the winner,
# cover_bunch how far (per cent) the other covers spread above the first.
cartels <- list(
  A = list(circle = "Rajgarh", firms = sprintf("K%02d", c(3, 5, 8, 11, 13, 14)),
           from = as.Date("2020-04-01"), to = as.Date("2022-09-30"),
           p_outsider = 0.15, cover_gap = c(1.5, 4.5), cover_bunch = 1.2),
  B = list(circle = "Tilakpur", firms = sprintf("K%02d", c(29, 31, 33, 34, 36, 38, 15)),
           from = as.Date("2022-04-01"), to = as.Date("2025-03-31"),
           p_outsider = 0.10, cover_gap = c(1, 4), cover_bunch = 2.5),
  # Planted. C is an incomplete cartel. Genuine outsiders bid in every one of its tenders.
  C = list(circle = "Udaygiri", firms = sprintf("K%02d", c(41, 43, 44, 46, 47)),
           from = as.Date("2021-07-01"), to = as.Date("2024-06-30"),
           p_outsider = 1, cover_gap = c(1.5, 4.5), cover_bunch = 1.2)
)

tenders <- tibble(circle = sample(circles, 880, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date("2020-04-01") + sample(0:1825, n(), replace = TRUE),
         work = sample(c("Road", "Building"), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)),
         estimate_lakh = round(rlnorm(n(), log(120), 0.7), 2)) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(tender_id = sprintf("PW-%03d", row_number()),
         fy = if_else(month(date) >= 4,
                      paste0(year(date), "-", year(date) %% 100 + 1),
                      paste0(year(date) - 1, "-", year(date) %% 100)),
         .before = 1)

# A genuine bid, in per cent above (+) or below (-) the estimate
genuine <- function(f, spread) unname(-7 + firm_habit[f] + rnorm(length(f), 0, spread))
draw_n <- function() sample(3:12, 1, prob = c(5, 16, 18, 17, 14, 11, 8, 6, 3, 2))

bid_list <- vector("list", nrow(tenders))
truth_list <- vector("list", nrow(tenders))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tenders))) {
  tn <- tenders[i, ]
  active <- keep(cartels, \(k) k$circle == tn$circle && tn$date >= k$from && tn$date <= k$to)
  # When a cartel is active, it takes part in about three tenders in four
  if (length(active) == 1 && runif(1) < 0.75) {
    k <- active[[1]]
    outsiders <- if (runif(1) < k$p_outsider) sample(1:2, 1) else 0
    n_members <- if (outsiders > 0) sample(3:5, 1) else sample(4:length(k$firms), 1)
    members <- sample(k$firms, n_members)
    out_firms <- sample(setdiff(pools[[tn$circle]], k$firms), outsiders)
    # The chosen winner bids high when alone, lower when outsiders may compete
    w <- if (outsiders == 0) rnorm(1, 1, 2.5) else rnorm(1, -5, 2)
    second <- w + runif(1, k$cover_gap[1], k$cover_gap[2])
    covers <- second + c(0, runif(n_members - 2, 0, k$cover_bunch))
    b <- tibble(firm = c(members, out_firms),
                quoted_pct = c(w, covers, genuine(out_firms, 3.5)))
    truth_list[[i]] <- tibble(tender_id = tn$tender_id, cartel = names(active),
                              incomplete = outsiders > 0)
  } else {
    # Genuine competition. How widely the bids spread differs from tender to tender.
    f <- sample(pools[[tn$circle]], draw_n())
    b <- tibble(firm = f, quoted_pct = genuine(f, runif(1, 2, 5)))
    truth_list[[i]] <- tibble(tender_id = tn$tender_id, cartel = "None", incomplete = FALSE)
  }
  bid_list[[i]] <- b |> mutate(tender_id = tn$tender_id, .before = 1)
}

truth <- bind_rows(truth_list)

bids <- bind_rows(bid_list) |>
  left_join(tenders, by = "tender_id") |>
  left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(bid_lakh = round(estimate_lakh * (1 + quoted_pct / 100), 2),
         collusive = cartel != "None") |>
  mutate(n_bids = n(), rank = rank(bid_lakh, ties.method = "first"), winner = rank == 1,
         .by = tender_id) |>
  select(tender_id, circle, work, date, fy, estimate_lakh, n_bids, firm, bid_lakh,
         rank, winner, collusive) |>
  arrange(date, tender_id, rank)

# Keep only the bids, and the truth that is used only for checking
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("bids", "truth")))
```

Let us look at the two tables.

```{r}
bids
truth
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_tenders <- n_distinct(bids$tender_id)
tl <- bids |> distinct(tender_id, n_bids, collusive)
n_coll <- sum(tl$collusive)
n_three <- sum(tl$n_bids == 3)
share_4to10 <- mean(tl$n_bids >= 4 & tl$n_bids <= 10)
n_incomplete <- sum(truth$incomplete)
```

There are `r format(nrow(bids), big.mark = ",")` bids in `r n_tenders` tenders. `r round(100 * share_4to10)`% of the tenders received four to ten bids, and `r n_three` received only three. `r n_coll` tenders are labelled collusive, and in `r n_incomplete` of them at least one genuine outsider also bid.

## The shape screens {#sec-bidshape-screens}

Seven screens are common in the research. Each one turns the bids of a tender into a single number. Let us write the bids of a tender in order, from the lowest, $b_1$, to the highest, $b_n$. The lowest bid wins.

- **Coefficient of variation (CV).** The standard deviation of the bids divided by their mean. Arranged bids often have a lower CV.
- **Spread.** The highest bid minus the lowest, divided by the lowest. A small spread means the bids are close together.
- **Percentage difference.** The gap between the two lowest bids, $(b_2 - b_1) / b_1$. It is the winner's lead over the runner-up.
- **Relative distance (RD).** The same gap, $b_2 - b_1$, divided by the standard deviation of the *losing* bids. A big gap above the winner, with tightly bunched losers, gives a high RD.
- **Normalised distance.** The same gap again, divided by the average gap between neighbouring bids. If the bids were evenly spaced, it would be 1. A value well above 1 means the winner stands apart.
- **Skewness.** Whether the bids lean to one side. A lone low winner below a bunch of losers gives a negative skew.
- **Kurtosis.** Whether the bids are bunched in the middle with a few far away. Bunched covers raise it.

For skewness and kurtosis we first turn each bid into a *standard score*, its distance from the mean in standard deviations. Skewness is the average of the cubes of these scores. Kurtosis is the average of their fourth powers, minus 3, so that a normal distribution gives zero. We use the simple divisor `n` here. The research papers use slightly adjusted formulas, which give a little different answers for small samples. Let us write the standard score as a small function.

```{r}
std_score <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))
```

### A tiny example

Here are two made-up tenders with five bids each, in ₹ lakh. In the first the firms compete. In the second, four covers sit bunched above the winner.

```{r}
example_bids <- tibble(
  tender = rep(c("Competitive", "Arranged"), each = 5),
  bid    = c(46.1, 47.9, 49.0, 50.8, 52.6,
             46.5, 49.4, 49.7, 50.0, 50.2)
)

example_bids |>
  arrange(tender, bid) |>
  summarise(cv     = sd(bid) / mean(bid),
            spread = (max(bid) - min(bid)) / min(bid),
            diffp  = (bid[2] - bid[1]) / bid[1],
            rd     = (bid[2] - bid[1]) / sd(bid[-1]),
            normd  = (bid[2] - bid[1]) / mean(diff(bid)),
            skew   = mean(std_score(bid)^3),
            kurt   = mean(std_score(bid)^4) - 3,
            .by = tender)
```

Because we sorted the bids, `bid[1]` is the winner and `bid[2]` the runner-up. `bid[-1]` is every bid except the winner, so `sd(bid[-1])` is the standard deviation of the losing bids. `diff(bid)` gives the gaps between neighbouring bids.

The arranged tender has a lower CV and a smaller spread. Its winner leads by more, so the percentage difference is larger. Its RD and normalised distance are much higher, its skew is negative and its kurtosis is higher. Every screen points the same way. With five bids, the difference is clear.

### How many bids does each screen need?

Each screen needs a minimum number of bids even to be calculated. @tbl-bidshape-minbids lists them.

| Screen | Needs at least | Why |
|-----------------------|----------------|---------------------------------------|
| Coefficient of variation | 2 bids | A standard deviation needs two numbers |
| Spread | 2 bids | Needs a highest and a lowest bid |
| Percentage difference | 2 bids | Needs a winner and a runner-up |
| Relative distance | 3 bids | Needs the standard deviation of at least 2 losing bids |
| Normalised distance | 3 bids | With 2 bids it is always exactly 1 |
| Skewness | 3 bids | Three numbers barely have a shape |
| Kurtosis | 4 bids | The research formula needs more than 3 bids |

: Minimum number of bids for each shape screen {#tbl-bidshape-minbids}

Being able to calculate a screen is not the same as it being useful. With three bids, the standard deviation of the two losing bids is little more than the gap between two numbers, so RD jumps about wildly. The research we meet in @sec-bidshape-research used only tenders with four or more bids, because kurtosis needs them. We shall do the same.

### The screens on our tenders

Now the same calculation for every tender. We sort the bids within each tender, and compute kurtosis only where there are at least four bids.

```{r}
shape <- bids |>
  arrange(tender_id, bid_lakh) |>
  summarise(n_bids = n(),
            cv     = sd(bid_lakh) / mean(bid_lakh),
            spread = (max(bid_lakh) - min(bid_lakh)) / min(bid_lakh),
            diffp  = (bid_lakh[2] - bid_lakh[1]) / bid_lakh[1],
            rd     = (bid_lakh[2] - bid_lakh[1]) / sd(bid_lakh[-1]),
            normd  = (bid_lakh[2] - bid_lakh[1]) / mean(diff(bid_lakh)),
            skew   = mean(std_score(bid_lakh)^3),
            kurt   = if (n() >= 4) mean(std_score(bid_lakh)^4) - 3 else NA,
            .by = c(tender_id, circle, fy, collusive))

shape
```

The `r n_three` tenders with three bids have no kurtosis. From here on we keep only the tenders with four or more bids, as the research did. To compare the screens, we also add from `truth` whether each tender was competitive, arranged by a complete cartel, or arranged by an incomplete one.

```{r}
shape4 <- shape |>
  filter(n_bids >= 4) |>
  left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(case = case_when(!collusive ~ "Competitive",
                          incomplete ~ "Incomplete cartel",
                          .default = "Complete cartel"))

shape4 |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), across(cv:kurt, \(x) round(median(x), 3)), .by = case)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
med <- shape4 |> summarise(n = n(), across(cv:kurt, median), .by = case)
mc <- med |> filter(case == "Competitive")
mk <- med |> filter(case == "Complete cartel")
mi <- med |> filter(case == "Incomplete cartel")
n_shape4 <- nrow(shape4)
```

The table shows the median of each screen. In the tenders of complete cartels, the median CV is `r round(mk$cv, 3)`, against `r round(mc$cv, 3)` in competitive tenders. The median RD is about `r sprintf('%.1f', mk$rd)`, against `r sprintf('%.1f', mc$rd)`. The skew is negative and the kurtosis higher. This is the signature the research describes. Collusion lowers the variation of the bids and makes them lopsided.

Now look at the incomplete cartel. Its tenders sit in between on almost every screen. Their median CV is `r round(mi$cv, 3)` and their median RD about `r sprintf('%.1f', mi$rd)`. The genuine outsiders spread the bids out again, and the signal fades. @fig-bidshape-box shows the whole distribution of each screen for the three kinds of tender.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bidshape-box
#| fig-cap: "The seven screens in competitive tenders and in the tenders of complete and incomplete cartels. Tenders with four or more bids."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "90%"
shape4 |>
  pivot_longer(cv:kurt, names_to = "screen", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(screen = fct_inorder(screen)) |>
  ggplot(aes(case, value, fill = case)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~screen, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

The boxes overlap. Some competitive tenders have a low CV or a high RD by chance. No single screen separates the groups cleanly.

### A simple rule

Before any model, let us try a simple rule of the kind an auditor might write by hand. We flag a tender when its CV is below 0.02 *and* its RD is above 1.5. These cut-offs are a judgement.

```{r}
shape4 |>
  mutate(flag = cv < 0.02 & rd > 1.5) |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), flagged = sum(flag), share = round(mean(flag), 2), .by = case)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rule <- shape4 |> mutate(flag = cv < 0.02 & rd > 1.5) |>
  summarise(n = n(), f = sum(flag), .by = case)
rc <- rule |> filter(case == "Competitive")
rk <- rule |> filter(case == "Complete cartel")
ri <- rule |> filter(case == "Incomplete cartel")
```

The rule flags `r rk$f` of the `r rk$n` tenders of complete cartels. It also flags `r rc$f` of the `r rc$n` competitive tenders. That is a small false alarm rate, but not zero. And it flags only `r ri$f` of the `r ri$n` tenders of the incomplete cartel. A rule built on the bids of the whole tender barely sees an incomplete cartel.

## What research shows {#sec-bidshape-research}

The screens are not our invention. A group of economists has tested them on real tenders where cartels were later proved.

::: callout-note
## What research shows

**Switzerland.** Martin Huber and David Imhof, "Machine learning with screens for detecting bid-rigging cartels", *International Journal of Industrial Organization*, vol. 65 (2019), pages 277 to 301 ([open full text](https://folia.unifr.ch/documents/309311/files/machinelearningwithscreensfordetectingbidriggingcartels.pdf?download)). They used 584 Swiss construction tenders with 3,799 bids. The Swiss Competition Commission had proved four cartels, so each tender was known to be collusive (in a cartel period) or competitive (after the cartel). Only tenders with four or more bids were used, because kurtosis needs more than three bids. In cartel tenders the mean kurtosis was 1.50 against 0.07 in competitive ones, the mean skewness -0.58 against 0.27, and the mean relative distance 2.69 against 0.83. They trained a lasso logit and an ensemble of bagged trees, random forests and neural networks, on 100 random splits into training and test data. About 84% of the test tenders were classified correctly. The lasso missed 14% of collusive tenders (false negatives) and wrongly flagged 18% of competitive ones (false positives). For the ensemble the figures were 17% and 15%. Tightening the rule to bring false positives down to about 10% pushed false negatives up to about 30%. The strongest screens were the gap between the two lowest bids, compared with the gaps among the bids, and the coefficient of variation. When these two were dropped, the models did not suffer much, as other screens stepped in. The authors propose a two-step procedure, screening first, then investigation.

**Japan.** Martin Huber, David Imhof and Rieko Ishii, "Transnational machine learning with screens for flagging bid-rigging cartels", *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A*, vol. 185, no. 3 (2022), pages 1074 to 1114 ([open full text](https://folia.unifr.ch/documents/330270/files/transnationalmachinelearningwithscreensforflaggingbid-riggingcartels_jounaloftheroyalstastisticalsociety.pdf)). They studied a cartel in Okinawa. Within Japan, 88 to 97% of tenders were classified correctly, depending on the model. The signature was the same as in Switzerland, lower variation and more asymmetry under collusion. But a model trained in one country and tested in the other did worse, because competitive bidding differs between the countries. Demeaning the screens, that is, adjusting them for each country's normal level, brought the ensemble to about 85 to 90%.

**Incomplete cartels.** Hannes Wallimann, David Imhof and Martin Huber, "A Machine Learning Approach for Flagging Incomplete Bid-Rigging Cartels", *Computational Economics* (2022), doi 10.1007/s10614-022-10315-w ([open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05629)). When some bidders are genuine competitors, the signal blurs. Their idea was to compute the screens for every subgroup of three or four bids in a tender, and use the mean, median, minimum and maximum across subgroups as predictors. With competitive bidders present, correct classification rose from roughly 61 to 77% with screens on all bids, to roughly 67 to 84% with the subgroups, depending on the case.
:::

These results are encouraging. But the models cannot simply be copied into Indian audit, for two plain reasons.

First, each model *learned from proven cartels*. It knows what those cartels' bids looked like. A cartel that works differently, with wider covers or more outsiders, may not look like anything the model has seen.

Second, *normal bidding differs* between countries and markets. Even the researchers found that a model trained in Switzerland did worse in Japan. Indian percentage-rate tenders start from a common Schedule of Rates, so genuine bids may cluster more tightly than in a market where each firm prices from scratch. A tight cluster that would be suspicious in one market may be ordinary in another. A model's cut-offs must be learnt from the market it is used in.

So we treat the research as a guide to *which screens matter and how to combine them*. The model itself must be built, and judged, on our own data.

## Subgroups of bids, for incomplete cartels {#sec-bidshape-subgroups}

When genuine outsiders bid, the cartel's bunched covers are still there, hidden among other bids. We do not know which bids are the cartel's. But we can look at *every* small group of bids in the tender. One of them will be the cartel's own.

### A tiny example

Here is a tender with six bids. Four come from a cartel, bunched above its chosen winner. Two come from genuine outsiders, one below and one above.

```{r}
mixed <- c(91.2, 95.0, 97.9, 98.3, 98.6, 103.4)
sd(mixed) / mean(mixed)
```

The CV of the whole tender is not especially low. `combn()` from base R lists every subgroup of a given size. Each column of its result is one subgroup.

```{r}
groups4 <- combn(mixed, 4)
dim(groups4)
groups4[, 1:3]
```

There are 15 subgroups of four bids among six. Let us find the CV of each, with `apply()`, which applies a function to each column (`2`) of a matrix.

```{r}
cv4 <- apply(groups4, 2, \(b) sd(b) / mean(b))
round(sort(cv4), 4)
groups4[, which.min(cv4)]
```

The subgroup with the lowest CV is the four cartel bids. Its CV is far below that of the whole tender. So for each tender we keep a few summaries of the subgroups, the mean, median, minimum and maximum of each screen. The minimum CV and the maximum RD are the natural candidates to catch a bunched group.

### Subgroup screens for all tenders

First we put the seven screens into one function. It returns a named vector, which is fast to compute many thousands of times. The formulas are the same as before.

```{r}
screen_values <- function(b) {
  b <- sort(b)
  n <- length(b)
  c(cv     = sd(b) / mean(b),
    spread = (b[n] - b[1]) / b[1],
    diffp  = (b[2] - b[1]) / b[1],
    rd     = (b[2] - b[1]) / sd(b[-1]),
    normd  = (b[2] - b[1]) / mean(diff(b)),
    skew   = mean(std_score(b)^3),
    kurt   = if (n >= 4) mean(std_score(b)^4) - 3 else NA)
}
screen_values(mixed)
```

The next function takes the bids of one tender and a subgroup size `k`. It computes the screens for every subgroup, drops kurtosis for subgroups of three, and returns the four summaries of each screen.

```{r}
subgroup_summary <- function(b, k) {
  v <- apply(combn(b, k), 2, screen_values)   # one column per subgroup
  v <- v[rowSums(is.na(v)) == 0, , drop = FALSE]
  out <- c(apply(v, 1, mean), apply(v, 1, median), apply(v, 1, min), apply(v, 1, max))
  names(out) <- paste0(rep(c("mean", "median", "min", "max"), each = nrow(v)),
                       k, "_", rownames(v))
  out
}
subgroup_summary(mixed, 4)[c("min4_cv", "max4_rd")]
```

Now we apply both sizes to every tender with four or more bids. `as_tibble_row()` turns the named vector into one row of columns. A tender with twelve bids has 495 subgroups of four, so this takes a few seconds.

```{r}
subs <- bids |>
  filter(n_bids >= 4) |>
  arrange(tender_id) |>
  summarise(as_tibble_row(c(subgroup_summary(bid_lakh, 3), subgroup_summary(bid_lakh, 4))),
            .by = tender_id)
dim(subs)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_sub_cols <- ncol(subs) - 1
```

Each tender now has `r n_sub_cols` subgroup screens.

### Does it help on the incomplete cartel?

A fair test must hold the false alarms steady. A subgroup's minimum CV is lower than the tender's CV in *every* tender, competitive or not. So comparing them against the same cut-off would mislead. Instead, for each screen we choose the cut-off that flags 10% of the competitive tenders. Then we see what share of each cartel's tenders it flags. We use the labels here, which is possible only because the data is simulated.

```{r}
compare <- shape4 |>
  left_join(subs, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(cv_all   = cv  < quantile(cv[!collusive], 0.10),
         min4_cv  = min4_cv < quantile(min4_cv[!collusive], 0.10),
         min3_cv  = min3_cv < quantile(min3_cv[!collusive], 0.10),
         rd_all   = rd  > quantile(rd[!collusive], 0.90),
         max3_rd  = max3_rd > quantile(max3_rd[!collusive], 0.90))

compare |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), across(c(cv_all, min4_cv, min3_cv, rd_all, max3_rd),
                                  \(x) round(mean(x), 2)), .by = case)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
cp <- compare |> summarise(across(c(cv_all, min4_cv, min3_cv, rd_all, max3_rd), mean), .by = case)
cpi <- cp |> filter(case == "Incomplete cartel")
cpk <- cp |> filter(case == "Complete cartel")
```

Each column is the share of tenders flagged by one screen, with the false alarms fixed at 10% of competitive tenders. On the incomplete cartel, the CV of all the bids flags `r round(100 * cpi$cv_all)`% of its tenders. The minimum CV over subgroups of four flags `r round(100 * cpi$min4_cv)`%, a modest gain. Over subgroups of three it flags `r round(100 * cpi$min3_cv)`%. RD on all bids flags `r round(100 * cpi$rd_all)`%, and the maximum RD over subgroups of three only `r round(100 * cpi$max3_rd)`%.

So, taken one at a time, the subgroup screens give little help, and some do worse. On the complete cartels they do much worse. The minimum CV over subgroups of four flags `r round(100 * cpk$min4_cv)`% of their tenders, against `r round(100 * cpk$cv_all)`% for the CV of all bids. A likely reason is this. A genuine tender with many bids also contains some subgroup of bids that happen to lie close together. So the minimum CV is low in many genuine tenders too, and the cut-off that holds false alarms at 10% must be very strict. What gives an incomplete cartel away may be not one summary but the contrast between them, one tight subgroup inside a tender that is otherwise spread out. A model can look at several summaries together. We will see what it makes of them in the next section.

## A random forest on the screens {#sec-bidshape-forest}

A model can weigh all the screens together, and learn cut-offs from the data. We use a random forest, as in @sec-forest. It is grown with `ranger()`, and gives each tender a score between 0 and 1, the share of trees voting "collusive".

### Training and test data

As in @sec-logistic, the model learns from 70% of the tenders and is judged on the other 30%, which it never saw. The predictors are the seven screens and the number of bids.

```{r}
model_data <- shape4 |>
  select(tender_id, collusive, n_bids, cv, spread, diffp, rd, normd, skew, kurt)

set.seed(11)
train_ids <- sample(model_data$tender_id, round(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data |> filter(tender_id %in% train_ids)
test  <- model_data |> filter(!tender_id %in% train_ids)
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

`ranger()` needs the outcome as a factor, and must not see `tender_id`, which is only a name.

```{r}
set.seed(12)
forest <- ranger(collusive ~ .,
                 data = train |> select(-tender_id) |> mutate(collusive = factor(collusive)),
                 num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE, importance = "permutation")

test <- test |>
  mutate(score = predict(forest, data = test)$predictions[, "TRUE"])
```

### The confusion table

We call a tender collusive when its score is above 0.5.

```{r}
table(predicted_collusive = test$score > 0.5, actually_collusive = test$collusive)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
cm <- table(factor(test$score > 0.5, c(FALSE, TRUE)), test$collusive)
n_test_coll <- sum(test$collusive)
n_test_comp <- sum(!test$collusive)
fa5 <- cm[2, 1] / n_test_comp
miss5 <- cm[1, 2] / n_test_coll
acc5 <- (cm[1, 1] + cm[2, 2]) / sum(cm)
```

Of the `r n_test_comp` competitive tenders in the test data, `r cm[2, 1]` were wrongly flagged. That is a **false alarm rate** of `r round(100 * fa5)`%. Of the `r n_test_coll` collusive tenders, `r cm[1, 2]` were missed. That is a **miss rate** of `r round(100 * miss5)`%. Overall, `r round(100 * acc5)`% of the test tenders were classified correctly. These are the false positive and false negative rates of the research, in plain words.

### Raising the cut-off

A false alarm costs the audit party time, and may cast doubt on honest firms. Raising the cut-off gives fewer of them, at a price. The function below gives both rates for any cut-off, as in @sec-logistic-evaluate.

```{r}
rates <- function(cutoff) {
  flagged <- test$score > cutoff
  tibble(cutoff,
         tenders_flagged  = sum(flagged),
         false_alarm_rate = round(mean(flagged[!test$collusive]), 2),
         miss_rate        = round(mean(!flagged[test$collusive]), 2))
}
map(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), rates) |> list_rbind()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
r3 <- rates(0.3)
r7 <- rates(0.7)
```

At a cut-off of 0.3, the forest misses `r round(100 * r3$miss_rate)`% of collusive tenders and raises false alarms on `r round(100 * r3$false_alarm_rate)`% of competitive ones. At 0.7, false alarms fall to `r round(100 * r7$false_alarm_rate)`%, but misses rise to `r round(100 * r7$miss_rate)`%. This is the same trade-off the Swiss study found. Fewer false alarms cost more missed cartels. There is no right cut-off. It depends on how many tenders the audit party can examine.

### Which cartels did it catch?

The overall rates hide an important detail. Let us split the test tenders by the truth.

```{r}
test |>
  left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), flagged = sum(score > 0.5), share = round(mean(score > 0.5), 2),
            .by = c(cartel, incomplete)) |>
  arrange(cartel)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bc <- test |> left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  summarise(n = n(), f = mean(score > 0.5), .by = c(cartel, incomplete))
bcA <- bc |> filter(cartel == "A", !incomplete)
bcB <- bc |> filter(cartel == "B", !incomplete)
bcC <- bc |> filter(cartel == "C")
```

The forest catches `r round(100 * bcA$f)`% of the complete tenders of cartel A and `r round(100 * bcB$f)`% of those of the sloppier cartel B. It catches only `r round(100 * bcC$f)`% of the tenders of cartel C, the incomplete cartel. Most of the misses are there.

### What did the forest rely on?

Permutation importance, explained in @sec-forest-inside, shows how much worse the forest gets when one screen is shuffled.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bidshape-importance
#| fig-cap: "Permutation importance of each screen in the random forest"
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "80%"
tibble(screen = names(forest$variable.importance),
       importance = forest$variable.importance) |>
  arrange(importance) |>
  ggplot(aes(importance, fct_inorder(screen))) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(x = "Loss in accuracy when the screen is shuffled", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
imp <- sort(forest$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)
```

Here the most important screens are `` `r names(imp)[1]` ``, `` `r names(imp)[2]` `` and `` `r names(imp)[3]` ``, and the least important is `` `r names(imp)[length(imp)]` ``. The Swiss study found the gap between the two lowest bids and the CV strongest. Our simulated cartels give a somewhat different order, which is a reminder that importance depends on the data. Several screens measure much the same thing, the tight cluster and the winner's lead. So when one is shuffled, the forest can lean on another. The Swiss study saw the same. Dropping its two strongest screens did not hurt much.

### Adding the subgroup screens

Now let us give the forest the subgroup screens as well, on exactly the same training and test tenders.

```{r}
train_sub <- train |> left_join(subs, by = "tender_id")
test_sub  <- test |> select(-score) |> left_join(subs, by = "tender_id")

set.seed(12)
forest_sub <- ranger(collusive ~ .,
                     data = train_sub |> select(-tender_id) |>
                       mutate(collusive = factor(collusive)),
                     num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)

test <- test |>
  mutate(score_sub = predict(forest_sub, data = test_sub)$predictions[, "TRUE"])

test |>
  left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  summarise(tenders = n(),
            all_bids  = round(mean(score > 0.5), 2),
            subgroups = round(mean(score_sub > 0.5), 2),
            .by = c(cartel, incomplete)) |>
  arrange(cartel)
```

The columns show the share of tenders flagged at a cut-off of 0.5, with screens on all bids and with subgroup screens added. For the competitive tenders (`None`) this share is the false alarm rate. For the cartels it is the share caught.

One split of the data can mislead, because the test set holds only a few tenders of each cartel. The researchers repeated their splits 100 times. Let us repeat ours 20 times, each with its own seed, and average.

```{r}
one_split <- function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  ids <- sample(model_data$tender_id, round(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
  fit_score <- function(d) {
    set.seed(s)
    f <- ranger(collusive ~ .,
                data = d |> filter(tender_id %in% ids) |> select(-tender_id) |>
                  mutate(collusive = factor(collusive)),
                num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)
    predict(f, data = d |> filter(!tender_id %in% ids))$predictions[, "TRUE"]
  }
  with_subs <- model_data |> left_join(subs, by = "tender_id")
  tibble(tender_id = setdiff(model_data$tender_id, ids),
         all_bids  = fit_score(model_data),
         subgroups = fit_score(with_subs))
}

repeated <- map(1:20, one_split) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(case = case_when(cartel == "None" ~ "Competitive",
                          incomplete ~ "Incomplete cartel",
                          .default = "Complete cartel"))

repeated |>
  summarise(predictions = n(),
            all_bids  = round(mean(all_bids > 0.5), 2),
            subgroups = round(mean(subgroups > 0.5), 2),
            .by = case)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rp <- repeated |> summarise(a = mean(all_bids > 0.5), s = mean(subgroups > 0.5), .by = case)
rpc <- rp |> filter(case == "Competitive")
rpk <- rp |> filter(case == "Complete cartel")
rpi <- rp |> filter(case == "Incomplete cartel")
rpC <- repeated |> filter(cartel == "C") |>
  summarise(a = mean(all_bids > 0.5), s = mean(subgroups > 0.5))
```

Over 20 splits, the forest on all-bid screens caught `r round(100 * rpi$a)`% of the incomplete cartel tenders. With the subgroup screens added, it caught `r round(100 * rpi$s)`%. That is a real gain, in the direction the 2022 study reported. It is not free. Catches of complete cartels went from `r round(100 * rpk$a)`% to `r round(100 * rpk$s)`%, and false alarms from `r round(100 * rpc$a)`% to `r round(100 * rpc$s)`%. And even with the subgroups, `r if (rpi$s < 0.75) paste0("about ", round(100 * (1 - rpi$s)), "% of the incomplete cartel's tenders are still missed") else "some of the incomplete cartel's tenders are still missed"`. A cartel that lets genuine firms bid remains hard to see from the bids alone.

### A harder test, a cartel the model has never seen

So far, every cartel had some tenders in the training data. In real use that is not so. The cartel an audit party most needs to find is one that nobody has found yet. Let us train on all tenders *except* those of one cartel, and then see how many of that cartel's tenders the forest flags.

```{r}
unseen <- map(c("A", "B", "C"), \(k) {
  d <- model_data |> left_join(truth |> select(tender_id, cartel), by = "tender_id")
  set.seed(13)
  f <- ranger(collusive ~ .,
              data = d |> filter(cartel != k) |> select(-tender_id, -cartel) |>
                mutate(collusive = factor(collusive)),
              num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)
  held_out <- d |> filter(cartel == k)
  tibble(cartel_left_out = k, tenders = nrow(held_out),
         caught = round(mean(predict(f, data = held_out)$predictions[, "TRUE"] > 0.5), 2))
}) |>
  list_rbind()
unseen
```

```{r}
#| include: false
uA <- unseen |> filter(cartel_left_out == "A")
uB <- unseen |> filter(cartel_left_out == "B")
uC <- unseen |> filter(cartel_left_out == "C")
```

When the forest has never seen cartel A, it still catches `r round(100 * uA$caught)`% of its tenders, probably because cartel B, which it has seen, bids in a similar way. For cartel B it catches `r round(100 * uB$caught)`%. For the incomplete cartel C, it catches only `r round(100 * uC$caught)`%. The forest learnt what *complete* cartels look like, and an incomplete one looks different. This is the plainest form of the warning in @sec-bidshape-research. A model learns the cartels it is shown. It may not recognise a cartel of a different kind.

::: callout-warning
## Caution

Our results are better than those in the research, for complete cartels at least. Do not read anything into that. Our data is simulated, and our cartels behave the same way in every tender. Real cartels are less tidy, real labels are fewer and less certain, and real competitive bidding has many more causes of tight or lopsided bids. On real data, expect the model to do worse than it does here.
:::

## Using the model responsibly {#sec-bidshape-responsible}

Everything above used labels. In a real audit, where could labels come from? There are three main sources, and each has limits.

- **Past audit findings.** Tenders where an earlier audit, with the department's later enquiry, established an arrangement. These are few, and they are the cases that were easy enough to find.
- **Orders of the Competition Commission of India.** The Commission has penalised bid rigging, including in tenders for the transport of coal and sand and in railway procurement. Under the Competition Act, 2002, bid rigging is presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition. Tenders named in such orders are proved cases. But they come from other markets, and normal bidding differs between markets.
- **Confessions and investigations.** Where a member of a cartel has confessed, or a vigilance or police investigation has established the facts, the tenders concerned are known. Again, these are few.

Labels from such sources are not a random sample. They over-represent cartels careless enough to be caught, and a model trained on them learns *those* cartels. The tenders without a label are not proven competitive either. They were simply not investigated.

Three rules follow.

1. **Use the score as a ranking, never as a finding.** A high score says "examine this tender before others". It does not say "this tender was rigged". The research itself proposes screening first, then investigation.
2. **Combine it with the other evidence.** The shape of the bids is one lens. The patterns across tenders of @sec-bidrig, such as who bids with whom, who wins in turn and how firms bid when outsiders appear, are another. The process flags of @sec-tenderflags, such as short bidding periods and restrictive conditions, are a third. A tender that stands out on two or three lenses deserves attention first.
3. **Do not use it on small tenders.** Most tenders in a district receive two to five bids. For them the shape screens are unreliable or cannot be calculated at all. Use the cross-tender screens of @sec-bidrig instead.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip

Without labels, the screens are still useful. Rank the tenders with four or more bids by a simple rule, such as low CV and high RD, or by an average of the ranks of several screens. Compare each circle with the others and with its own past, as the Japanese study did when it adjusted for each country's normal level. A model trained on labels is a further step, worth taking only when there are enough proved cases from a similar market.
:::

## Audit use case, ranking a year's larger tenders for examination {#sec-bidshape-ranking}

The audit party is planning the audit of 2024-25. It has the bids of every tender of the year. Suppose that earlier audits and enquiries had established which tenders of 2020-21 to 2023-24 were arranged. (In our data, these are the labels.) It wants to rank the larger tenders of 2024-25, so that the team can examine the riskiest first.

We train the forest, with the subgroup screens, on the earlier years only, and score 2024-25.

```{r}
all_screens <- model_data |>
  left_join(subs, by = "tender_id") |>
  left_join(shape4 |> select(tender_id, fy, circle), by = "tender_id")

past <- all_screens |> filter(fy != "2024-25")
this_year <- all_screens |> filter(fy == "2024-25")

set.seed(14)
forest_past <- ranger(collusive ~ .,
                      data = past |> select(-tender_id, -fy, -circle) |>
                        mutate(collusive = factor(collusive)),
                      num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)

ranked <- this_year |>
  mutate(score = predict(forest_past, data = this_year)$predictions[, "TRUE"]) |>
  select(tender_id, circle, n_bids, cv, rd, score) |>
  arrange(desc(score))

head(ranked, 15)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_year <- nrow(ranked)
top <- ranked |> slice_head(n = 15)
top_circ <- top |> count(circle, sort = TRUE)
year_value <- bids |> filter(tender_id %in% top$tender_id, winner) |> pull(bid_lakh) |> sum()
```

There are `r n_year` tenders of 2024-25 with four or more bids. The team decides it can examine 15. Of the top 15, `r top_circ$n[1]` are in `r top_circ$circle[1]`. The winning bids of the 15 add up to ₹`r round(year_value / 100, 2)` crore.

Now we bring in the cross-tender view of @sec-bidrig. Which firms bid in these top 15 tenders, and how often?

```{r}
bids |>
  filter(tender_id %in% top$tender_id) |>
  count(firm, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
top_firms <- bids |> filter(tender_id %in% top$tender_id) |> count(firm, sort = TRUE)
core <- top_firms$firm[top_firms$n >= 5]
core_wins <- sum(bids$winner & bids$tender_id %in% top$tender_id & bids$firm %in% core)
```

The same few firms appear again and again. `r length(core)` firms each bid in at least five of these 15 tenders, and between them they won `r core_wins` of the 15. A small set of firms meeting in many high-scoring tenders, and sharing the wins, is exactly the pattern that @sec-bidrig tests for rotation and for the margin of covers.

Because the data is simulated, we can check what the ranking found.

```{r}
ranked |>
  left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(group = if_else(row_number() <= 15, "Top 15", "Rest")) |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), collusive = sum(cartel != "None"), .by = group)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
chk <- ranked |> left_join(truth, by = "tender_id") |>
  mutate(group = if_else(row_number() <= 15, "top", "rest")) |>
  summarise(n = n(), c = sum(cartel != "None"), .by = group)
chk_top <- chk |> filter(group == "top")
chk_rest <- chk |> filter(group == "rest")
```

`r chk_top$c` of the top 15 tenders were in fact collusive. `r chk_rest$c` collusive tenders were left among the other `r chk_rest$n`. In a real audit we would not know this. We would know only that these tenders deserve to be examined first.

### What the auditor does next

1. **Check the tenders against the cross-tender screens** of @sec-bidrig. For the firms of the top-ranked tenders, test who bids with whom, the order of wins and the margin of covers, over all their tenders and not only the large ones.
2. **Check the process** of each top-ranked tender against the flags of @sec-tenderflags, such as the bidding period, the qualification conditions and any retendering.
3. **Get the full tender records.** These include the comparative statements, the earnest money details with the bank accounts they came from, and the upload times of the bids on the e-procurement portal.
4. **Compare the bid documents** for the same mistakes, the same layout or the same file properties.
5. **Record the method in the working papers.** Note the screens, the training years, the source of the labels, the seed, and the cut-off or the number of tenders chosen, before the tenders are examined.
6. **Report patterns, not conclusions.** State what the bids and the records show, and recommend that the department examine the matter and, where it sees fit, refer it to the competent authority.

## A suggested workflow

1. **Keep the tenders with four or more bids.** The shape screens are unreliable, or cannot be calculated, on smaller ones. Use the cross-tender screens of @sec-bidrig for those.
2. **Compute the seven screens** for each tender by hand, with sorted bids.
3. **Look at their distributions**, by circle and by year, and try a simple rule such as low CV and high RD.
4. **Add subgroup screens** with `combn()` where genuine outsiders may hide a cartel.
5. **Train a model only if there are labels** from a similar market. Split into training and test data, with seeds, and repeat the split.
6. **Report the false alarm and miss rates** at the chosen cut-off, and the trade-off when it is raised.
7. **Test on a cartel the model has not seen**, if there are enough proved cases.
8. **Rank the tenders for examination**, and combine the ranking with the cross-tender patterns and the process flags.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- The shape screens need four or more bids. Kurtosis needs four, and skewness and relative distance need three. Most small tenders cannot be screened this way.
- Collusion tends to lower the variation of bids and to set the winner apart from bunched covers. Genuine tenders can look the same by chance.
- An incomplete cartel, with genuine outsiders bidding, blurs the signal. Screens on subgroups of three or four bids help, but do not solve it.
- A model learns the cartels it is shown. It may miss a cartel of a different kind, and normal bidding differs between markets.
- Real audits rarely have labels. Where they exist, they are few and not a random sample.
- Raising the cut-off cuts false alarms and raises misses. Choose it for the number of tenders the team can examine.
- Use the score to rank tenders for examination, never as proof.
:::

## Where next

The patterns across tenders, which work even with two or three bids, are in @sec-bidrig. The red flags in the tendering process are in @sec-tenderflags. Random forests, their settings and variable importance are explained in @sec-forest, and training and test data, the confusion table and cut-offs in @sec-logistic. A single decision tree, which is easier to explain to a department, is in @sec-trees. Other ways to find unusual records without labels are in @sec-anomaly.

## Try it yourself {#sec-bidshape-exercises}

These exercises use the tables `bids` and `truth`, and the objects `shape4`, `model_data`, `train`, `test`, `subs` and `screen_values()` of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.

1.  **One tender by hand.** Find the tender with the most bids. Compute its seven screens with `screen_values()`, and check the CV against the value in `shape4`.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_id <- bids |> slice_max(n_bids, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(tender_id)
    ex_bids <- bids |> filter(tender_id == ex_id) |> pull(bid_lakh)
    ex_vals <- screen_values(ex_bids)
    round(ex_vals, 3)
    shape4 |> filter(tender_id == ex_id) |> select(tender_id, n_bids, cv, rd)
    ```
    Tender `r ex_id` has `r length(ex_bids)` bids. Its CV is `r format(round(ex_vals[["cv"]], 3), nsmall = 3)` by both routes, as it should be, since the formulas are the same.
    :::

2.  **A stricter rule.** Flag tenders with CV below 0.015 and RD above 2. Count the flags for each kind of tender in `shape4`, and compare with the rule in the chapter.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_rule <- shape4 |>
      mutate(flag = cv < 0.015 & rd > 2) |>
      summarise(tenders = n(), flagged = sum(flag), .by = case)
    ex_rule
    ```
    The stricter rule flags `r ex_rule$flagged[ex_rule$case == "Competitive"]` competitive tenders and `r ex_rule$flagged[ex_rule$case == "Complete cartel"]` tenders of complete cartels. Fewer false alarms, and more misses. The same trade-off appears with a hand-made rule as with a model.
    :::

3.  **An even higher cut-off.** Using the scores in `test`, find the false alarm rate and the miss rate at a cut-off of 0.8.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_flag <- test$score > 0.8
    ex_fa <- mean(ex_flag[!test$collusive])
    ex_miss <- mean(!ex_flag[test$collusive])
    round(c(false_alarm_rate = ex_fa, miss_rate = ex_miss), 2)
    ```
    At 0.8, the false alarm rate is `r round(100 * ex_fa)`% and the miss rate `r round(100 * ex_miss)`%. The Swiss study found the same pattern. Tightening its rule to cut false positives to about 10% raised false negatives to about 30%.
    :::

4.  **Without the two strongest screens.** Find the two most important screens of `forest`. Grow the forest again on `train` without them, and compare the share of test tenders classified correctly with the forest of the chapter.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_drop <- names(sort(forest$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
    ex_drop
    set.seed(12)
    ex_forest <- ranger(collusive ~ .,
                        data = train |> select(-tender_id, -all_of(ex_drop)) |>
                          mutate(collusive = factor(collusive)),
                        num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE)
    ex_score <- predict(ex_forest, data = test)$predictions[, "TRUE"]
    ex_acc <- c(full = mean((test$score > 0.5) == test$collusive),
                reduced = mean((ex_score > 0.5) == test$collusive))
    round(ex_acc, 3)
    ```
    The full forest classifies `r round(100 * ex_acc[["full"]], 1)`% of the test tenders correctly. Without `` `r ex_drop[1]` `` and `` `r ex_drop[2]` ``, the forest classifies `r round(100 * ex_acc[["reduced"]], 1)`% correctly. The other screens step in, as in the Swiss study, because they measure much the same thing.
    :::

5.  **Examining the top tenth.** Sort the test tenders by `score`. What share of all the collusive tenders in the test data falls in the top 10% of scores?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_top <- test |>
      arrange(desc(score)) |>
      mutate(top_tenth = row_number() <= round(0.1 * n()))
    ex_caught <- sum(ex_top$collusive & ex_top$top_tenth) / sum(ex_top$collusive)
    c(examined = sum(ex_top$top_tenth), collusive_caught = sum(ex_top$collusive & ex_top$top_tenth))
    ```
    Examining the top `r sum(ex_top$top_tenth)` tenders would reach `r round(100 * ex_caught)`% of the collusive tenders in the test data. There are `r sum(ex_top$collusive)` collusive tenders in the test data, more than the `r sum(ex_top$top_tenth)` places. So even a perfect ranking could reach at most `r round(100 * sum(ex_top$top_tenth) / sum(ex_top$collusive))`% of them. The forest comes close to that limit.
    :::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `sd()`, `mean()`, `diff()` | stats, base R | CV, spread, the gaps between bids, and the standard scores for skewness and kurtosis |
| `arrange()`, `summarise(.by = )` | dplyr | Sorts the bids within each tender and computes the screens tender by tender |
| `combn()` | utils | Lists every subgroup of three or four bids in a tender |
| `apply()` | base R | Applies the screens to each subgroup, and summarises each screen across subgroups |
| `as_tibble_row()` | tibble | Turns a named vector of screens into one row of a table |
| `quantile()` | stats | Sets the cut-off that flags a fixed share of competitive tenders |
| `sample()`, `set.seed()` | base R | Splits the tenders into training and test data, reproducibly |
| `ranger()`, `predict()` | ranger | Grows the random forest and scores new tenders |
| `table()` | base R | The confusion table of predicted against actual |
| `map()`, `list_rbind()` | purrr | Repeats the split, and leaves out each cartel in turn |
| `pivot_longer()` | tidyr | Puts the screens in one column for the box plots |
| `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_col()` | ggplot2 | Compares the screens by kind of tender, and shows variable importance |
